The battlefield. The majority places the President in Category 1; the dissent says Category 3, "at best" Category 2. The majority also cites it for the proposition — which nobody disputes — that no granted power may be exercised in a way that deprives individuals of constitutional rights.
424 U.S. 319 (1976)In your files

Mathews v. Eldridge — disability benefits, cut off without a hearing

What happened
George Eldridge received Social Security disability benefits. A state agency reviewed his file, sent him a questionnaire, obtained reports from his physician and a psychiatric consultant, and tentatively concluded his disability had ended. He was given a summary of the evidence and an opportunity to respond in writing. Benefits were terminated. He was entitled to a full evidentiary hearing afterward, with retroactive relief if he won.
Held
An evidentiary hearing is not required before termination. The existing procedures satisfied due process.
The test it created
"[I]dentification of the specific dictates of due process generally requires consideration of three distinct factors:"
First, the private interest that will be affected by the official action. Second, the risk of an erroneous deprivation through the procedures used, and the probable value, if any, of additional or substitute safeguards. Third, the government's interest, including the function involved and the fiscal and administrative burdens the additional procedure would entail.
What to notice about it
Two things. It is a balancing test, so it rarely produces bright lines. And it was created in a case where the claimant lost — the Court found that disability determinations turn on relatively objective medical evidence, reducing error risk, and that the recipient wasn't in the same desperate position as the welfare recipient in Goldberg v. Kelly. Mathews is not a plaintiff-friendly test by design.
Its role here
Both opinions apply it, via Hamdi. Everything depends on factor one — Hamdi says freedom from physical restraint is "the most elemental of liberty interests" — and on whether the government's asserted burden (disclosure would compromise national security) is treated as an ordinary administrative cost or as something categorically different.
542 U.S. 507 (2004)In your files

Hamdi v. Rumsfeld — the American captured in Afghanistan

What happened
Yaser Hamdi, born in Louisiana and raised in Saudi Arabia, was seized in Afghanistan by the Northern Alliance and turned over to the U.S. military, which alleged he was a Taliban fighter. He was taken to Guantanamo; when his American citizenship was discovered he was moved to a naval brig in Virginia. He was held without charge, without counsel, and without any hearing. The government's entire evidentiary submission was a short declaration from a Defense Department official — the "Mobbs Declaration."
Held — split two ways
On authority: the AUMF authorized his detention. Detention of enemy combatants for the duration of the relevant conflict is a "fundamental incident of waging war" and therefore falls within "necessary and appropriate force."
On process: a citizen-detainee seeking to challenge his classification must receive notice of the factual basis for that classification and a fair opportunity to rebut the government's assertions before a neutral decisionmaker.
The accommodations the plurality allowed
It is not an ordinary criminal trial. Hearsay may be accepted. A rebuttable presumption may be applied in favor of the government's evidence, so long as the detainee has a fair chance to rebut it. The plurality suggested a properly constituted military tribunal could satisfy the requirement.
The line everyone quotes
"[A] state of war is not a blank check for the President when it comes to the rights of the Nation's citizens."
The vote — know this before a judge asks
O'Connor announced the judgment; her opinion is a plurality of four (with Rehnquist, Kennedy, Breyer). Souter, joined by Ginsburg, concurred in part and dissented in part — they thought the detention was not authorized at all under the Non-Detention Act, but joined to give Hamdi a remand. Scalia, joined by Stevens, dissented: a citizen must be charged with treason or another crime, or Congress must suspend habeas — no third option. Thomas dissented the other way: the detention was a valid exercise of war powers and the plurality gave insufficient deference.
So: eight Justices agreed Hamdi could not be held on the process he received, for two incompatible reasons. Lower courts treat the plurality's process holding as controlling.
Its role here
The template for the likely outcome and the case both sides need. Note the two structural distinctions the government presses: Hamdi was a citizen, and he was captured in an active combat zone. Bronner is neither.
115 F.4th 928 (8th Cir. 2024)Not in your files

Banyee v. Garland — the circuit case both sides claim

What it addresses
Prolonged immigration detention and when due process requires additional procedure. Not binding on the Supreme Court, and the only source for it in your materials is how the two opinions below characterize it.
How the majority uses it
Courts have not categorically banned detentions longer than six months, nor held that detainees are entitled to an "individual determination" of each detention decision — especially absent evidence the detention is a "ruse to incarcerate [him] for other reasons."
How the dissent uses it
Even where statutes authorize detention, due process may require periodic review to prevent detention from becoming effectively indefinite. The dissent presents it as proof that courts can craft procedures protecting security and liberty at once.
Why it matters
It is the only place in the record where a concrete remedy short of release is described. Any judge looking for a way to rule for Bronner without dismantling war powers will reach for periodic review, and this is where it comes from.

title: Applied to Bronner
html:
Applied to Bronner — what each fact does

Pushes toward "exceeded his authority"
  • Thirty years of continuous lawful residence; entered at fifteen as an asylee. R. 4
  • Naturalization approved Feb 17, 2025, with an express good moral character finding. Oath scheduled July 4; military transfer July 7. R. 4, 8
  • No prior convictions. The AG classified him as having a "criminal record" because he had been accused. R. 8
  • Arraigned in an Article III court, pled not guilty, released on bond — the exact Milligan situation, and evidence that the error risk under Mathews factor two is not hypothetical. R. 8; dissent R. 19
  • Twelve months in military custody, uncharged, on sealed evidence he has never seen. R. 7–8
  • ATA § 4 supplies no time limit, no dangerousness finding, no counsel, no judicial review. R. 3; App. V (R. 24)
  • ATA § 4(b)(1) permits offshore detention only for the unlawfully present; § 4(b)(2) requires citizens be held inside. Bronner falls in neither. R. 3; App. V (R. 24)
  • A 2026 House bill to authorize offshore detention of lawfully present non-citizens is still pending in the Senate — Congress is presently deciding whether to grant the power the President claims he already has. R. 3
  • NDAA § 1021(b)(2) requires a connection to al-Qaeda, the Taliban, or associated forces. The record says the sellers were questioned about suspected ties to organizations involved in drug smuggling. That is several inferential steps short of the statutory element, and it concerns them, not him. R. 7; App. III (R. 21)
  • The President's signing-ceremony statement that inherent powers allow him to act "beyond any specific law or statutory framework." R. 3–4
Pushes toward "within his authority"
  • Sealed warehouse documents the government says show an arranged purchase of a radiological weapon. R. 7–8
  • Roper and Langbourne: foreign convictions for selling military-grade arms; questioned twice by federal agents about terrorist ties. R. 7
  • Fentanyl patches, lollipops, spray, a sales log, four boxes of lozenges in the car — the drug case is strong on its own. R. 7
  • Independent NSA surveillance separately observed the warehouse meeting. R. 7
  • NDAA § 1021(a) affirms detention authority; § 1021(c)(1) expressly permits detention without trial until hostilities end. This is affirmative statutory text and it is the government's best card. App. III (R. 21); R. 13
  • § 1022(b) exempts citizens and lawful residents from the requirement of military custody — arguably lifting an obligation, not a power. App. IV (R. 22); R. 2
  • § 1021(d) and (e) and ATA § 4(c): nothing limits or expands existing authority — which keeps the field open and argues against Category 3. R. 21, 24; discussed R. 2–3, 14
  • 10 U.S.C. § 948(a)(7)(B) covers those who purposefully and materially support hostilities. App. II (R. 20); R. 12
  • Senate efforts to bar indefinite detention failed repeatedly; AUMF repeal failed in 2023 and 2025; a signing statement asserted the power and Congress did not respond. R. 3
  • Quirin: neither citizenship nor arrest on U.S. soil is disqualifying. R. 12
  • Habeas is functioning — he filed, won below, and is before the Supreme Court. R. 8–9, 14
  • Government states it intends to try him as soon as practicable; delay is attributed to evidence sensitivity, not punishment. R. 8, 14
Where this question actually lands

Read Hamdi carefully and the shape of the likely answer appears: the authority argument is winnable for the government and the process argument is winnable for Bronner. Hamdi split exactly that way — the AUMF authorized detention, and the process Hamdi received was constitutionally insufficient.

Two distinctions decide whether Hamdi transfers. Citizenship: Hamdi's process holding is framed for "a citizen-detainee," but the Fifth Amendment's word is "person," and lawful permanent residents within the United States have long been held to have due process rights. Capture location: Hamdi was seized in an active combat zone where belligerency was evidenced by circumstance; Bronner was arrested at home by civilian police and arraigned. That second distinction cuts toward more process, not less — the further you get from a battlefield, the weaker the case for battlefield rules.

The two record wrinkles on Question 2

1. Section numbering. Page 3 of the record attributes the "nothing shall be construed to affect existing law" language to § 1022(e); the dissent attributes it to § 1021(e); Appendix III shows it at § 1021(e). Appendix IV (§ 1022) has no subsection (e) at all. Cite Appendix III.

2. The AG's stated reason. He classified Bronner as a non-citizen "with a criminal record" because he had been "accused." That is a misuse of the term. But EO 15,000 covers non-citizens with criminal records or pending criminal charges, and Bronner had pending charges. The order's terms are arguably satisfied even though the AG's stated reason is wrong. Both sides should know which of those they're talking about.

title: The hinge
html:
The hinge: Question 1 is load-bearing for Question 2

The two questions look independent. A chain of stipulations connects them, and noticing it is worth more than any single doctrinal point.

  1. The parties stipulate that the government relied primarily on the pole-camera footage to establish probable cause for the warrants.
  2. Footnote 8: the government did not assert it had probable cause without that footage. That is a waiver.
  3. The warrants produced the search of the warehouse.
  4. The warehouse produced the sealed documents.
  5. The sealed documents are the only basis for calling Bronner an unprivileged enemy belligerent — the fentanyl is drug evidence, not terrorism evidence.

If the pole-camera surveillance was an unlawful search, the documents fall — and the only thing making Bronner a belligerent rather than a drug defendant falls with them.

Why this helps Bronner
  • It converts Question 2 from a war-powers abstraction into a question about the reliability of an executive determination — which is Mathews factor two.
  • It raises the stakes on Question 1: this is not a suppression motion about fentanyl, it is the origin of a twelve-month detention.
  • Footnote 8 forecloses the independent source exception, which is normally the government's escape from fruit-of-the-poisonous-tree.
The government's answers, and their weaknesses
  • Separate the questions. Article II asks whether the President had authority; the lawfulness of underlying evidence is a suppression issue that does not travel into a habeas challenge to detention authority. This is a clean answer and probably the right one doctrinally.
  • Point to the NSA. Agents Bourgeois and Quinlan observed the warehouse meeting independently. Weakness: they declined to disclose their purpose or intelligence, so by definition none of it is in the record. You cannot build an independent-source argument from something nobody would describe.
  • Note what remains. Even without the documents, the fentanyl evidence supports an ordinary prosecution. Weakness: that is precisely Bronner's point — an ordinary prosecution is what an Article III court had already begun.

html:
The numbers and names worth knowing cold

title: Glossary
html:
Glossary — plain English, no jargon defined with jargon

Search (Fourth Amendment)
Not rummaging. The government learning something you were entitled to keep to yourself. No touching or entry required. If it isn't a search, the Amendment is silent.
Reasonable expectation of privacy
Two halves: did you treat it as private, and will society protect it? The second half decides cases.
Curtilage
The yard immediately around a house — porch, steps, the fenced part. Treated as part of the home.
Sense-enhancing technology not in general public use
Kyllo's trigger. A device ordinary people don't have, used to learn about a home's interior.
Mosaic theory / aggregation
Many individually harmless observations combine into something that isn't. Never adopted by name in a Supreme Court majority; Tuggle says lower courts are not required to apply it.
Third-party doctrine
The idea that information you hand to someone else (a bank, a phone company) loses Fourth Amendment protection. Carpenter declined to extend it to cell-site records.
Fruit of the poisonous tree
Evidence found because of an illegal search is usually excluded too. Escapes: independent source (they had it another way), inevitable discovery (they'd have found it anyway), attenuation (the link is too remote).
Good faith exception
Evidence isn't suppressed when police reasonably relied on then-binding precedent or a facially valid warrant. It is why Moore-Bush reversed even though three judges found a search.
Habeas corpus
"Produce the body." A petition asking a court to make the government justify holding someone. Tests the detention, not the charge.
Writ
A court order. "Granting the writ" here means ordering the government to justify or end the detention.
Article III court
An ordinary federal court with a life-tenured judge. Contrast: a military commission, whose members are officers.
Military commission
A military tribunal that tries offenses against the law of war. At issue in Quirin and Milligan. Bronner has not been tried by one — he hasn't been tried at all.
Unprivileged enemy belligerent
A statutory label, not a fact. Someone who fights or materially supports fighting against the U.S. without the protections lawful combatants get. The label unlocks detention without trial.
Lawful vs. unlawful belligerent
Quirin's distinction. Lawful (uniformed) combatants are held as prisoners of war. Unlawful ones — fighting in civilian clothes behind the lines — may additionally be tried and punished.
Law of war detention
Holding a captured fighter until hostilities end. Prevention, not punishment — hence no trial requirement.
Youngstown categories
Congress said yes (maximum) / said nothing (zone of twilight) / said no (lowest ebb). A map of how much authority a President has for a given act.
Dictum
A line in an opinion not necessary to the decision. Not binding. Curtiss-Wright's "sole organ" is the example here — Jackson said so in Youngstown footnote 2.
Congressional acquiescence
The claim that long silence ratifies executive practice. Requires a consistent, longstanding construction and meaningful silence.
Signing statement
A president's written comment on signing a bill, often reserving a constitutional objection. Not law; evidence of executive position.
Non-delegation
The principle limiting how much lawmaking power Congress may hand the executive. The actual issue in Curtiss-Wright.
Due process
Not a right to win. A right to be told why, and to argue back, before someone neutral.
Mathews balancing
Three factors: the private interest; the error risk plus the value of more procedure; the government's interest including burden.
De novo review
The reviewing court decides the legal question fresh, owing nothing to the court below.
Stipulated
Both sides agreed. You cannot dispute it.
Preserved / not preserved
An argument raised properly below is available on appeal; one that wasn't is gone. Footnotes 8 and 9 wall off several.
Waiver
Giving up an argument, deliberately or by not making it.
Plurality
The largest group agreeing on reasoning, but fewer than five. Hamdi's process language is a plurality of four.
Concurrence in the judgment
Agreeing on the outcome but not the reasoning. Why Youngstown's Jackson concurrence, not its majority, is what courts use.
Per curiam
"By the court" — an unsigned opinion. Moore-Bush's one-paragraph judgment is per curiam because no rationale commanded a majority.
En banc
The full circuit rehearing a case decided by a three-judge panel. Vacates the panel opinion.
Certiorari
The Supreme Court's discretionary agreement to hear a case. Granting it signals the question is thought important or unsettled.

title: Corrections & gaps
html:
Corrections and remaining gaps

Correction to the earlier version of this guide

I described Moore-Bush as a 3–3 split that left the district court affirmed by an equally divided court. That is wrong. The en banc First Circuit issued a per curiam judgment unanimously reversing the suppression order. The 3–3 division is over the reasoning: Barron, Thompson, and Kayatta held it was a search but reversed on the good-faith exception (because circuit precedent, Bucci, had said otherwise); Lynch, Howard, and Gelpí held it was not a search.

Practical consequence: the case is not authority that pole-camera surveillance requires suppression. It is authority that the constitutional question divides serious judges evenly — and that even a court finding a search may decline to suppress.

The Eighth Amendment label

You originally described these as the Eighth Amendment table of authorities. There is no Eighth Amendment issue in this case — no cruel-and-unusual-punishment question, no sentencing question. Q1 is Fourth Amendment; Q2 is Article II plus Fifth Amendment due process.

Still not in your files

You now have every case the two opinions cite except these:

  • Banyee v. Garland, 115 F.4th 928 (8th Cir. 2024) — cited by both opinions for opposite propositions. The only source of the periodic-review remedy.
  • United States v. Bucci, 582 F.3d 108 (1st Cir. 2009) — the precedent Moore-Bush was about overruling, and the source of the "no fences, gates, or shrubbery" reasoning the government's brief will echo.
  • United States v. Houston, 813 F.3d 282 (6th Cir. 2016) — the source of the "possibility, not practicability" fiction that Tuggle rejected and the trial court in Tafoya relied on.
  • United States v. Knotts, 460 U.S. 276 (1983) — the "augment the sensory faculties bestowed upon them at birth" line.
  • State v. Jones, 903 N.W.2d 101 (S.D. 2017) — two months of pole-camera surveillance of street-visible activities held to be a search. On the split table above, this is the single most useful non-binding case for Bronner, because it is the only one finding a search without a fence doing the work.

Worth reading if your rules permit citing outside the case file: Boumediene v. Bush, 553 U.S. 723 (2008) (habeas extends to Guantanamo — though jurisdiction is stipulated here) and Zivotofsky v. Kerry, 576 U.S. 1 (2015) (rejecting the "sole organ" reading of Curtiss-Wright). Check the AMCA rules first.
